content: H7N2 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, commonly referred to as a bird flu virus. In 2002, one individual in Virginia, United States, was found to have serologic evidence of H7N2 infection. Similarly, in 2003, another individual in New York, United States, was identified with serologic evidence of infection. Both individuals fully recovered from the illness. In February 2004, an outbreak of low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) H7N2 was reported on two chicken farms in Delaware. Additionally, the virus was detected in four live bird markets in New Jersey that were supplied by the same farms. In March 2004, surveillance testing of a chicken flock in Maryland also confirmed the presence of LPAI H7N2. It is highly probable that this was the same strain involved in the earlier outbreaks. A study conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) following the 2002 outbreaks in commercial poultry farms in western Virginia provided further insights into the epidemiology of the virus. On May 24, 2007, an outbreak of H7N2 was confirmed at a poultry farm near Corwen, Wales. The infection was identified through testing of chickens that had died from the virus. The farm owners had purchased 15 Rhode Island Red chickens two weeks prior, all of which succumbed to H7N2. The remaining 32 poultry at the site were culled to prevent further spread of the virus. Authorities established a one-kilometer exclusion zone around the property, restricting the movement of birds and bird products. Bird gatherings within the zone were only permitted under specific licensing conditions. Nine individuals who had been in contact with the infected or deceased poultry reported experiencing flu-like symptoms. Of these, four tested positive for H7N2 infection. All affected individuals were successfully treated and experienced only mild flu symptoms. In early June 2007, it was discovered that the virus had spread to another poultry farm located approximately 70 miles (113 kilometers) away near St. Helens in north-west England. All poultry at this farm were culled, and a one-kilometer exclusion zone was implemented to contain the outbreak.
